lesson.title: Who Are PSRs for?
lesson.summary: Understand who are psrs for from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Professional Practice
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 14–18
stage.description: Objects and patterns in the wider project: version control, testing, and automated builds.

payload.markdown: Ostensibly, PSRs are designed for the creators of frameworks. The fact that the membership of the PHP-FIG group rapidly widened to include the creators of tools as well as frameworks, however, shows that standards have wide relevance. That said, unless you are creating a logger, you may not need to worry too much about the details of PSR-3 (beyond ensuring any logging tool you use is itself compliant). On the other hand, if you’ve read the rest of this book, chances are you are as likely to be creating tools as you are to be consuming them. So, it’s also likely that you’ll find something relevant to you either in the present standards or the standards to come.

payload.markdown: And then there are the standards that matter to all of us. Unglamorous as style guides are, for example, they are relevant to every programmer. And while the rules that govern autoloading really apply to those who create autoloaders (and the main game in town is probably Composer’s), they also fundamentally affect how we organize our classes, our packages, and our files. For these reasons, I will focus on coding style and autoloading for the rest of this chapter.

items: Autoloading & Composer: Loading classes on demand by PSR-4 rules; Composer wires it up.
Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
PSR-1/12/4: PHP standards for coding style, file structure and autoloading.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
CLI Tools: Running PHP from the terminal: plain scripts, Composer scripts and REPL tools.
